subject: chemistry-2
question: A chemistry exercise calls for preparing exactly 0.5 mol of glucose (C6H12O6, molar mass 180.16 g/mol). Which mass should be weighed out, and why?

options.text: 180.16 g, because the molar mass is the mass to weigh whenever a mole quantity is specified
360.32 g, because the molar mass is divided by the requested mole quantity
90.08 g, because mass equals the requested moles multiplied by the molar mass
0.00278 g, because the requested moles are divided by the molar mass

explanation:
Converting moles to mass uses mass = moles x molar mass, so 0.5 mol x 180.16 g/mol = 90.08 g. The units confirm the setup, since moles multiplied by grams per mole leaves grams. Dividing instead produces 360.32 g or 0.00278 g, both of which fail the estimation check that half a mole must weigh half of the molar mass.

ELI-10: If one full container of a substance weighs 180.16 grams, half a container weighs half that, which is 90.08 grams. That is the whole calculation: moles times molar mass. Build in the estimate before you compute. When the requested amount is less than one mole, the mass must come out smaller than the molar mass; when it is more than one mole, the mass must come out larger. An answer that breaks this rule means the multiplication was flipped into a division.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
